The Story of King Sagar

I bow to Lord Jinendra, worshipped by the gods, and I write the story of the second Chakravartin, Sagar.

In the famous and beautiful Videha region of Jambudvip, to the east of the Sita River, lies the land of Vatsakavati. Its ancient capital was Prithivi-nagar, ruled by King Jaysen. His queen was Jaysena. They had two sons, Ratisen and Dhritisen. Both brothers were handsome and virtuous. But by the cruel march of time, Ratisen died. Jaysen was deeply grieved, and in that grief, he gave the kingdom to Dhritisen and, along with kings Marut and Mithun, took initiation from the monk Yashodhar and became a monk. They practised austerities for many years, then died as monks and were reborn in heaven — Jaysen as the great god Mahabal, and Marut as the god Maniketu, who was a devoted servant of the Lord's lotus feet. These two gods, enjoying heavenly bliss, made a pact in their love of dharma: whoever was reborn as a human first should go to the other in heaven and guide him toward detachment and Jain initiation.

Mahabal's lifespan was twenty-two sagar (oceanic periods). He enjoyed heavenly pleasures to his heart's content. When his time was complete, through the residual merit he was born as Sagar, son of King Samudravijay and Queen Subala of Ayodhya. His age was seventeen lakh purva years, and his golden body stood four hundred and fifty bows tall — that is, 1,575 hands high. All the beauty of the world had made its home in him. He was so handsome that all who beheld him were filled with joy.

Sagar conquered all six continents and became the second Chakravartin. But with power and wealth, he forgot his dharma. He had sixty thousand sons. He had family, wealth, bodily splendour, and every comfort. Time passed in great happiness. Truly, through merit, living beings attain all manner of excellent possessions. Therefore, the wise should use their wealth and power for dharma, not for indulgence.

One day, the god Maniketu came to Sagar in the guise of a monk and reminded him of his spiritual duty. He spoke of the impermanence of worldly pleasures and the supreme value of the soul's liberation. Sagar was struck by these words. He realised that despite all his power and wealth, he was still bound by karma and subject to birth and death. He renounced his kingdom, became a monk, and practised intense austerities. Through dedicated spiritual practice, he destroyed his karmas and attained liberation.

This story teaches that even the greatest worldly power and beauty are impermanent. King Sagar had everything a person could desire — yet he was still subject to suffering and rebirth. It was only when he turned toward dharma that he found true peace. The wise should not be deluded by worldly success but should use their opportunities to practise dharma and attain liberation.
